title: JSON: data that travels
hook: Read and write the format every app and website uses.

warmup.explain: Every CSV cell is text, even a number. Convert it with `int()` or `float()` before adding.

warmup.q: What does opening a file with mode `"a"` do?
options: Adds to the end and keeps what was there
warmup.explain: `"a"` is append. `"w"` is the one that erases.
Square brackets crash on a missing key. `.get` is the safe way.

why.heading: The language apps speak
why.text: Apps, websites and tools swap data as **JSON**. It looks almost like a Python dictionary and list: `{"shot": "1A", "mins": 20}`. Learn it once and you can read data from almost anything, including the web tools next week.

why.heading: Text in, data out
why.text: JSON is only text until you load it. `json.loads(text)` turns the text into real Python dicts and lists. `json.dumps(data)` goes the other way, data to text. The `s` stands for string.

why.heading: Straight to files
why.text: `json.load(f)` with no `s` reads straight from an open file. `json.dump(data, f)` writes to one. Add `indent=2` to dump or dumps and the text comes out neat, one key per line, easy for you to read.

why.heading: Data inside data
why.text: JSON nests: a list of dictionaries, a dictionary holding a list. Dig in one step at a time. `shots[0]["mins"]` is the first shot, then its minutes. If you get lost, print each step.

why.heading: Small differences
why.text: JSON writes `true`, `false` and `null`. Python calls them `True`, `False` and `None`. The conversion is automatic. JSON also insists on double quotes, never single quotes.

watch.intro: Tap Run. It loads a slate from a JSON file, bumps the take number, shows it neatly and saves a new file.
watch.code:
import json
with open("slate.json") as f:
    slate = json.load(f)
print(slate["scene"])
slate["take"] += 1
print(json.dumps(slate, indent=2))
with open("slate_new.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(slate, f, indent=2)
explain: `json.load(f)` read the file and gave back a normal Python dictionary.
We changed the take with `+= 1`, exactly like any dictionary.
`json.dumps(..., indent=2)` made text with one key per line. Notice `true` is lower case.
`json.dump(slate, f, indent=2)` wrote the same neat text into slate_new.json.
watch.break_it: Change `json.load(f)` on line 3 to `json.loads(f)` (add an s) and tap Run. You get a `TypeError`, because `loads` wants text, not an open file. Take the s off again.

tasks.title: Read a call time
tasks.task:
`call.json` holds one small dictionary. Read the whole file as text with `f.read()`, turn it into data with `json.loads`, then show the unit and the call time:

`Imvana call: 06:00`
tasks.starter:
import json
with open("call.json") as f:
    text = f.read()
data = json.loads(text)
print(data)
tasks.solution:
import json
with open("call.json") as f:
    text = f.read()
data = json.loads(text)
print(data["unit"], "call:", data["call"])
hints: `data` is now a dictionary. Printing it shows curly brackets and quotes.
Look up the two keys: `data["unit"]` and `data["call"]`.

tasks.title: Total the shots
tasks.task:
`shots.json` is a list of dictionaries. Show each shot and its minutes, then the total minutes:

`1A 20`
`1B 30`
`2A 15`
`Total: 65`
tasks.starter:
import json
with open("shots.json") as f:
    shots = json.load(f)
total = 0
for s in shots:
    print(s["shot"])
print("Total:", total)
tasks.solution:
import json
with open("shots.json") as f:
    shots = json.load(f)
total = 0
for s in shots:
    print(s["shot"], s["mins"])
    total += s["mins"]
print("Total:", total)
hints: Each `s` is a dictionary with the keys `shot` and `mins`. Print both on one line.
Also add the minutes to `total`. In JSON a number is already a number, so no int() needed.
Inside the loop: print(s["shot"], s["mins"]) and then total += s["mins"]

tasks.title: Add a crew member and save
tasks.task:
`crew.json` is a list of people. Add `{"name": "Kay", "role": "Boom"}` to the end, save the list back into `crew.json` with `indent=2`, and show how many people there are now, like:

`Crew now: 3`
tasks.starter:
import json
with open("crew.json") as f:
    crew = json.load(f)
crew.append({"name": "Kay", "role": "Boom"})
print("Crew now:", len(crew))
# save it back here
tasks.solution:
import json
with open("crew.json") as f:
    crew = json.load(f)
crew.append({"name": "Kay", "role": "Boom"})
print("Crew now:", len(crew))
with open("crew.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(crew, f, indent=2)
hints: Saving means opening the file again, this time to write.
Open with mode "w", then use json.dump(crew, f, indent=2).
with open("crew.json", "w") as f:  then  json.dump(crew, f, indent=2)

recap: JSON is the text format apps use. It looks like Python dictionaries and lists.
`json.loads(text)` and `json.dumps(data)` convert between text and data.
`json.load(f)` and `json.dump(data, f)` do the same straight with a file. `indent=2` makes it neat.
Dig into nested data one step at a time: `shots[0]["mins"]`.
